topicName: Categorical Encoding: OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder, and TargetEncoder
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Categorical Encoding in Scikit-learn"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Machine learning models require numerical input data. When working with tabular datasets, categorical variables often represent qualitative attributes that cannot be directly ingested by algorithms like linear regression, support vector machines, or neural networks. Scikit-learn provides robust preprocessing utilities to transform categorical features into numeric formats. This tutorial explores three essential encoders: OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder, and TargetEncoder."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. OneHotEncoder"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"OneHotEncoder creates a binary column for each category present in the feature. If a sample belongs to a specific category, its corresponding binary column is set to 1, while all other columns for that feature are set to 0. This approach prevents algorithms from assuming an artificial mathematical ordering among categories."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

data = pd.DataFrame({"City": ["New York", "London", "Paris", "London"]})
encoder = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, drop="first")
encoded_data = encoder.fit_transform(data)
print(encoded_data)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. OrdinalEncoder"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"OrdinalEncoder maps categorical strings to integer values sequentially (0, 1, 2, ...). This technique is ideal for ordinal data where a clear logical hierarchy or ranking exists, such as educational levels or satisfaction ratings (Low, Medium, High)."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

data = pd.DataFrame({"Education": ["High School", "Bachelor", "Master", "PhD"]})
category_order = [["High School", "Bachelor", "Master", "PhD"]]
encoder = OrdinalEncoder(categories=category_order)
encoded_data = encoder.fit_transform(data)
print(encoded_data)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. TargetEncoder"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"TargetEncoder replaces each category with the shrunk average of the target variable for that category. This method is exceptionally powerful for high-cardinality categorical features (e.g., zip codes or product IDs) because it embeds statistical target information directly into the feature without expanding dimensionality."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

X = pd.DataFrame({"Category": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "C"]})
y = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
encoder = TargetEncoder(smooth="auto")
encoded_data = encoder.fit_transform(X, y)
print(encoded_data)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Summary"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use OneHotEncoder for nominal data with low to moderate cardinality to avoid multicollinearity (use drop='first')."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use OrdinalEncoder strictly when categories have a natural mathematical or logical order."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use TargetEncoder for high-cardinality features in supervised regression or classification tasks while ensuring proper cross-validation to prevent data leakage."}]
